stem:
A cart's velocity changes from 2 m/s to 8 m/s in 3 s. Its average acceleration is

A. 2 m/s²
B. 3 m/s²
C. 6 m/s²
D. 10 m/s²

rationales.A: Average acceleration = (8-2 m/s)/3 s = 2 m/s².
rationales.B: Mistakes the initial velocity value (2 m/s) for a time value, computing (8-2)/2 = 3 m/s² instead of correctly dividing by the actual 3 s interval given in the problem.
rationales.C: Reports the raw velocity change (8-2 m/s) without dividing by the elapsed time at all.
rationales.D: Adds the initial and final velocities (2+8) instead of subtracting them to get the change.

stem:
A 4 kg block has a net horizontal force of 12 N. Its acceleration is

A. 0.33 m/s²
B. 3 m/s²
C. 8 m/s²
D. 48 m/s²

rationales.A: Inverts the Newton's-second-law division, computing mass over force (4/12) instead of force over mass.
rationales.B: Newton's second law gives 12/4
rationales.C: Subtracts mass from force (12-4) instead of dividing force by mass.
rationales.D: Multiplies force by mass (12x4) instead of dividing, treating F=ma as a=Fm.

stem:
A book rests on a table. The Newton's-third-law partner to the table's force on the book is

A. Earth's force on the book
B. book's force on the table
C. table's weight
D. book's inertia

rationales.A: Confuses the third-law pair with the book's weight, a separate force that also acts on the book itself rather than the reaction to the table's normal force.
rationales.B: third-law forces act on different objects
rationales.C: Substitutes the table's own weight, a force from gravity on the table, for the reaction force the book exerts on the table.
rationales.D: Mistakes inertia, a property of the book's mass, for a force, so it cannot be a Newton's-third-law partner at all.

stem:
A block slides down a rough incline at constant speed. Along the incline, friction is

A. zero
B. less than downhill gravity
C. equal to downhill gravity
D. greater than downhill gravity

rationales.A: Assumes that because the block keeps moving there must be no friction, mistaking constant velocity for the absence of a friction force.
rationales.B: Assumes friction only partially opposes the gravity component since the block is still moving, missing that constant speed requires the parallel forces to be exactly balanced.
rationales.C: zero acceleration requires balanced parallel forces
rationales.D: Assumes friction must exceed the gravity component to explain why the block isn't speeding up, missing that constant (not decreasing) speed instead requires the two forces to be equal.

stem:
A constant 10 N force moves an object 3 m in its direction. The work is

A. 3 J
B. 13 J
C. 30 J
D. 300 J

rationales.A: Reports the distance alone (3 m relabeled as joules), forgetting to multiply by the applied force.
rationales.B: Adds the force and distance (10+3) instead of multiplying them.
rationales.C: W=Fd cos 0
rationales.D: Introduces an extra spurious factor of 10 into the F times d product, as if a units conversion were needed.

stem:
If an object's speed doubles, its kinetic energy becomes

A. half
B. double
C. four times
D. eight times

rationales.A: Assumes kinetic energy scales inversely with speed, as if doubling speed reduced KE.
rationales.B: Assumes kinetic energy scales linearly with speed, forgetting the square in KE=(1/2)mv^2.
rationales.C: kinetic energy is proportional to speed squared
rationales.D: Assumes kinetic energy scales with the cube of speed, over-applying the exponent as if it were 3 instead of 2.

stem:
A 2 kg object falls 5 m near Earth. The decrease in gravitational potential energy is about

A. 10 J
B. 20 J
C. 50 J
D. 100 J

rationales.A: Drops g entirely, computing just mass times height (2x5) as if g=1.
rationales.B: Computes only the weight mg (2x9.8) and forgets to multiply by the height fallen.
rationales.C: Drops the mass factor, computing just g times h (9.8x5) as if the object had 1 kg mass.

stem:
During a collision, equal and opposite impulses imply that the two objects have

A. equal speed changes
B. equal mass
C. equal-magnitude momentum changes
D. equal kinetic energies

rationales.A: Assumes equal momentum changes imply equal speed changes, ignoring that unequal masses would give unequal Deltav for the same Deltap.
rationales.B: Treats equal-and-opposite impulses as a statement about the objects' masses rather than about the forces and time of contact they share.
rationales.C: impulse equals momentum change
rationales.D: Assumes equal momentum changes give equal kinetic energy changes, ignoring that KE depends on v-squared and mass, which can split unevenly between the objects.

stem:
For ideal simple harmonic motion, acceleration is

A. constant
B. proportional to displacement and opposite it
C. proportional to velocity
D. zero at all times

choices.label: B
choices.text: proportional to displacement and opposite it

rationales.A: Treats SHM acceleration like free-fall's constant acceleration, ignoring that it depends on the changing displacement.
rationales.B: a=-ω²x
rationales.C: Confuses SHM's restoring-force relation with a damping-type relation, wrongly linking acceleration to velocity instead of to displacement.
rationales.D: Overgeneralizes the fact that acceleration is zero at equilibrium to claim it is zero throughout the whole motion.

stem:
A mass-spring oscillator has maximum speed at

A. maximum positive displacement
B. maximum negative displacement
C. equilibrium
D. every position equally

rationales.A: Assumes speed peaks at the turning point, where the oscillator is actually momentarily at rest.
rationales.B: Makes the same turning-point error on the opposite side, assuming maximum speed at maximum compression rather than at momentary rest there.
rationales.C: potential energy is minimum at equilibrium
rationales.D: Assumes speed stays constant through the oscillation, ignoring the continuous exchange between kinetic and potential energy.

stem:
A passenger lurches forward when a car stops because

A. a forward force appears
B. inertia preserves forward motion
C. the seat removes mass
D. gravity points forward

rationales.A: Incorrectly assumes a new forward force acts on the passenger; the passenger continues moving forward because of inertia while the car slows.
rationales.B: the passenger tends to maintain velocity
rationales.C: Attributes the lurch to a nonphysical loss of mass rather than to the passenger's own inertia continuing forward.
rationales.D: Misattributes the lurch to a change in gravity's direction rather than to the passenger's tendency to keep moving at the car's original velocity.

stem:
A force does negative work on an object when it

A. is perpendicular to displacement
B. has a component opposite displacement
C. is larger than weight
D. acts for less than one second

choices.label: D
choices.text: acts for less than one second

rationales.A: Assumes any misalignment between force and displacement gives negative work, when a purely perpendicular force actually does zero work.
rationales.B: the dot product is negative for an opposing component
rationales.C: Ties the sign of work to the force's magnitude relative to weight rather than to the angle between force and displacement.
rationales.D: Ties the sign of work to the duration the force acts rather than to the direction of the force relative to the displacement.

stem:
A satellite of mass m orbits a planet of mass M in a circular orbit of radius r. Which expression gives the satellite's orbital speed?

A. √(GM/r)
B. √(2GM/r)
C. √(GM/r²)
D. √(GMm/r)

rationales.A: Setting gravitational force equal to centripetal force, GMm/r² = mv²/r, and solving for v gives v = √(GM/r).
rationales.B: This is the escape-velocity expression, obtained by setting total mechanical energy to zero rather than by equating gravitational force to centripetal force (GMm/r^2 = mv^2/r) -- a common mix-up between two related but distinct derivations.
rationales.C: This has units under the square root that do not simplify to velocity units (m/s); the r in the denominator should be r¹, not r².
rationales.D: This carries an uncancelled factor of the satellite's own mass m. In the correct derivation, GMm/r^2 = mv^2/r, the satellite mass m appears on both sides and cancels before solving for v; an expression that still contains m has not completed that cancellation.

stem:
For a satellite in a circular orbit around a planet, how does the orbital period T depend on the orbital radius r?

A. T ∝ r^(1/2)
B. T ∝ r
C. T ∝ r^(3/2)
D. T ∝ r²

rationales.A: This matches the square-root form of a simple pendulum's period (T=2π√(L/g)), a formula students often misapply here by pattern-matching "period involves a square root of a length," rather than deriving T from v=√(GM/r) and T=2πr/v, which actually gives T∝r^(3/2).
rationales.B: This ignores that orbital speed v decreases as r increases, which makes T increase faster than linearly with r.
rationales.C: Since T = 2πr/v and v = √(GM/r), substituting gives T = 2π r^(3/2)/√(GM), so T is proportional to r^(3/2).
rationales.D: This overstates how quickly the period grows with radius; the correct relationship from T = 2πr/v with v = √(GM/r) gives r^(3/2), not r².

stem:
Two satellites orbit the same planet in circular orbits. Satellite 1 has a smaller orbital radius than Satellite 2. The two satellites have different masses. How do their orbital speeds compare?

A. Satellite 1 has a greater orbital speed than Satellite 2.
B. Satellite 1 has a smaller orbital speed than Satellite 2.
C. The two satellites have the same orbital speed.
D. The comparison cannot be determined without knowing the satellites' masses.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Satellite 1 has a greater orbital speed than Satellite 2.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Satellite 1 has a smaller orbital speed than Satellite 2.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The two satellites have the same orbital speed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The comparison cannot be determined without knowing the satellites' masses.

rationales.A: Orbital speed v = √(GM/r) depends only on the planet's mass M and orbital radius r, not on the satellite's own mass; since Satellite 1 has the smaller radius, it has the greater orbital speed.
rationales.B: This reverses the r-dependence: orbital speed decreases as radius increases, so the satellite with the smaller radius has the greater, not smaller, speed.
rationales.C: Orbital speed depends on radius through v = √(GM/r); since the two satellites orbit at different radii, their speeds cannot be equal.
rationales.D: The satellites' own masses cancel out of v = √(GM/r) — orbital speed depends only on the planet's mass and the orbital radius, both of which are already given here.

stem:
A bicycle's velocity decreases uniformly from 12 m/s to 0 in 4.0 s. How far does it travel while stopping?

A. 12 m
B. 24 m
C. 6 m
D. 48 m

rationales.A: This uses the initial speed times one second and ignores the four-second interval.
rationales.B: The triangular area under velocity versus time is (1/2)(4.0 s)(12 m/s)=24 m.
rationales.C: This reports the calculated average speed as distance without multiplying by the four-second travel time.
rationales.D: This uses the full rectangle 12×4, as if velocity stayed at 12 m/s.

stem:
A ball rolls horizontally from a 20 m-high ledge at 5.0 m/s. Neglect air resistance and use g=10 m/s². How far from the ledge does it land?

A. 5.0 m
B. 10 m
C. 20 m
D. 7.1 m

rationales.A: This uses a one-second fall time, omitting the square-root calculation from vertical motion.
rationales.B: The fall time is sqrt(2h/g)=2.0 s, so horizontal range is (5.0)(2.0)=10 m.
rationales.C: This treats the 20 m vertical height as though it were the horizontal range.
rationales.D: This uses t = sqrt(h/g), omitting the factor of 2 from vertical motion; falling 20 m from rest takes 2.0 s, not about 1.41 s.

stem:
Train A moves east at 30 m/s while Train B moves east at 20 m/s. What is A's velocity relative to B?

A. 10 m/s east
B. 10 m/s west
C. 50 m/s east
D. 50 m/s west

rationales.A: For same-direction motion, v_A/B=30-20=10 m/s east.
rationales.B: This subtracts the speeds but reverses the relative direction.
rationales.C: This adds same-direction velocities, which is appropriate for opposite-direction closing speed.
rationales.D: This both adds the speeds and assigns the direction opposite A's motion.

stem:
A truck collides with a small car. During contact, which comparison of interaction forces is correct?

A. Truck on car is larger
B. Car on truck is larger
C. Forces are equal in magnitude and opposite
D. Forces are equal only if masses match

choices.label: C
choices.text: Forces are equal in magnitude and opposite

choices.label: D
choices.text: Forces are equal only if masses match

rationales.A: This infers force from vehicle size, confusing force equality with differing accelerations.
rationales.B: This is Newton's third-law pair; unequal masses produce unequal accelerations, not unequal forces.
rationales.C: Newton's third law gives equal-magnitude opposite forces on the two different vehicles.
rationales.D: This wrongly makes the third-law equality depend on equal masses.

stem:
At a distance r from a planet's center the gravitational field is g₀. At distance 2r it is

A. 4g₀
B. 2g₀
C. g₀/2
D. g₀/4

rationales.A: This applies direct-square scaling instead of inverse-square scaling.
rationales.B: This assumes field is directly proportional to radius rather than inversely proportional to radius squared.
rationales.C: This applies an inverse-linear relation and misses the square on distance.
rationales.D: The inverse-square relation g=GM/r² makes doubling radius reduce the field to g₀/4.

stem:
A horizontal push on a stationary crate increases from zero but remains below the threshold for slipping. The friction force

A. is always μ_sN
B. matches the push in magnitude
C. is zero until slipping
D. equals μ_kN

rationales.A: This treats the maximum μ_sN as the friction value for every subthreshold push.
rationales.B: Static friction adjusts to match the applied push until its maximum value is reached.
rationales.C: This ignores static friction, which acts before any slipping begins.
rationales.D: This uses the kinetic-friction formula even though the crate remains stationary.

stem:
An ideal horizontal spring is stretched 0.15 m to the right of equilibrium. If k=80 N/m, the spring force on the attached block is

A. 12 N right
B. 12 N left
C. 6.8 N left
D. 0 N

rationales.A: This calculates the correct magnitude but drops the restoring-force direction encoded by the negative sign.
rationales.B: Hooke's law F=-kx gives magnitude 12 N directed left, opposite the rightward displacement.
rationales.C: This uses an unrelated remaining distance instead of multiplying the spring constant by the 0.15 m displacement.
rationales.D: This assumes force vanishes away from equilibrium rather than at equilibrium.

stem:
A rider moves through the bottom of a vertical circular track at speed v. Which radial equation is correct if inward is upward?

A. N+mg=mv²/r
B. N-mg=mv²/r
C. mg-N=mv²/r
D. N=mg

rationales.A: This adds weight as inward even though weight points outward/downward at the bottom.
rationales.B: At the bottom, inward is upward, so the inward net force is N-mg=mv²/r.
rationales.C: This reverses the net-force signs and would describe inward as downward.
rationales.D: This imposes vertical equilibrium despite the required centripetal acceleration.

stem:
Masses 1.0 kg and 3.0 kg are at x=0 and x=4.0 m, respectively. The center of mass is at

A. 1.0 m
B. 2.0 m
C. 3.0 m
D. 4.0 m

rationales.A: This places the center near the smaller mass by reversing the mass weighting.
rationales.B: This takes the unweighted midpoint and ignores the unequal masses.
rationales.C: x_cm=(1×0+3×4)/(1+3)=3.0 m, closer to the larger mass.
rationales.D: This places the center exactly on the 3.0 kg mass rather than between the masses.

stem:
If an object's speed triples while its mass is unchanged, its translational kinetic energy becomes

A. 3 times as large
B. 6 times as large
C. 9 times as large
D. unchanged

rationales.A: This assumes kinetic energy is directly proportional to speed and misses the square.
rationales.B: This multiplies the speed factor by two instead of squaring it.
rationales.C: Because K=(1/2)mv², tripling v multiplies kinetic energy by 3²=9.
rationales.D: This ignores the speed dependence in the kinetic-energy expression.

stem:
A 50 N force pulls a crate 4.0 m while directed 60° above the horizontal displacement. The work by this force is

A. 0 J
B. 100 J
C. 173 J
D. 200 J

rationales.A: This treats the entire angled force as perpendicular to the displacement, even though its horizontal component does work.
rationales.C: This uses sin60° instead of the component parallel to horizontal displacement.
rationales.D: This uses Fd without accounting for the 60° angle.

stem:
In one dimension, a conservative force points in the +x direction throughout a region. As x increases, potential energy

A. increases
B. decreases
C. stays constant
D. must be zero

rationales.A: This assumes force points toward increasing potential rather than down the potential-energy landscape.
rationales.B: A positive force points toward decreasing potential energy, so U decreases as x increases.
rationales.C: This would require zero force, contradicting the stated nonzero +x force.
rationales.D: This confuses the arbitrary zero of potential energy with its spatial change.

stem:
A bead starts from rest at height h above the bottom of a frictionless track. Its speed at the bottom is

A. 2sqrt(gh)
B. sqrt(gh)
C. sqrt(2gh)
D. sqrt(gh/2)

rationales.A: This incorrectly treats sqrt(2) as 2 when solving the energy equation.
rationales.B: This omits the factor of two arising from the one-half in kinetic energy.
rationales.C: Conservation of energy mgh=(1/2)mv² gives v=sqrt(2gh).
rationales.D: This places the factor of one-half on the wrong side when applying conservation of energy.

stem:
A 70 kg student climbs 3.0 m vertically in 5.0 s. Using g=10 m/s², the average power is

A. 210 W
B. 140 W
C. 420 W
D. 2100 W

rationales.A: This incorrectly uses an average height of h/2 instead of the full 3.0 m vertical rise.
rationales.B: This omits the 3.0 m height and divides weight by time.
rationales.C: Average power=mgh/t=(70)(10)(3.0)/5.0=420 W.
rationales.D: This calculates the gravitational energy but fails to divide by elapsed time.

stem:
A block slides down a rough ramp and reaches the bottom slower than an identical block on a frictionless ramp. For the rough-ramp system, the missing mechanical energy primarily becomes

A. gravitational potential energy
B. thermal energy
C. momentum
D. sound energy

rationales.A: Both blocks finish at the same bottom height, so the slower block does not retain gravitational potential energy.
rationales.B: Kinetic friction transforms mechanical energy into thermal energy of the block and ramp.
rationales.C: This confuses a vector motion quantity with the form into which energy is transferred.
rationales.D: Sound accounts for only a small fraction; friction primarily converts the missing mechanical energy to thermal energy.

stem:
A uniform disk and a thin ring have the same mass and radius. The same tangential force is applied at each rim. Compared with the ring's angular acceleration, the disk's angular acceleration is

A. twice as large
B. the same
C. half as large
D. four times as large

rationales.A: The torques match, while I_disk=(1/2)MR² and I_ring=MR², so α_disk is twice α_ring.
rationales.B: Equal torque does not give equal angular acceleration when the rotational inertias differ.
rationales.C: This reverses the inverse relationship between angular acceleration and rotational inertia.
rationales.D: This incorrectly squares the factor-of-two difference in rotational inertia, as though angular acceleration were proportional to 1/I² rather than 1/I.

stem: An object's acceleration-time graph shows the acceleration increasing linearly with time (nonuniform acceleration). According to the AP Physics 1 course framework, which of the following is a student expected to be able to do for this situation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Calculate the exact instantaneous velocity at a given time using integration of the acceleration function.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Qualitatively sketch a velocity-time graph that is consistent with the given acceleration-time graph.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Determine an exact algebraic equation for velocity as a function of time using the three constant-acceleration kinematic equations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Treat the acceleration as effectively zero for the purposes of analysis.

rationales.A: AP Physics 1 is algebra-based; calculus techniques such as integration are never required or expected on this exam. (Though related non-calculus techniques, such as finding areas under acceleration-time graphs, are within scope for related skills.)
rationales.B: The CED states students are not expected to quantitatively analyze nonuniform acceleration, but are expected to qualitatively analyze, sketch, and discuss such situations.
rationales.C: The three kinematic equations (v=v0+at, etc.) apply only to constant-acceleration situations; they cannot be used directly for nonuniform acceleration.
rationales.D: Nonuniform acceleration is changing over time; treating it as zero would misrepresent the given situation entirely.

stem: On a free-response question requiring a numerical answer, a student uses g = 9.8 m/s^2 instead of g = 10 m/s^2 for all calculations, and carries this value through correctly and consistently. What is the effect on the student's score for that question?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A one-point deduction is applied for using an incorrect constant.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No penalty is applied; both g = 10 m/s^2 and the more precise values g = 9.8 m/s^2 or 9.81 m/s^2 are acceptable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Full credit is awarded only if the final numeric answer is rounded to match the result obtained using g = 10 m/s^2.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The response is disqualified from earning credit on that question.

rationales.A: AP Physics 1 does not penalize the use of the more precise value; there is no deduction for this choice.
rationales.B: The CED explicitly states that while g=10 m/s^2 is used for all situations requiring a numerical value, students will not be penalized for correctly using the more precise commonly accepted values of 9.8 or 9.81 m/s^2.
rationales.C: There is no requirement to match the g=10 result; a correctly and consistently carried-through 9.8 or 9.81 value is fully acceptable on its own terms.
rationales.D: This is far too severe; the CED explicitly permits either value with no penalty.

stem: According to the AP Physics 1 course framework, adding or subtracting velocity vectors to find an object's velocity as measured from a different reference frame (e.g., a boat's velocity relative to the ground, given the boat's velocity relative to the water and the water's velocity relative to the ground) is a skill that is:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Required in full two-dimensional generality, including cases where the two velocities are not along the same line.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Restricted to situations in which the velocities being combined are along the same one-dimensional line.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Not covered at all in the AP Physics 1 course.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tested only using calculus-based vector methods.

rationales.A: The CED explicitly restricts this skill to one dimension for AP Physics 1, not full 2-D generality.
rationales.B: The CED states that adding or subtracting vectors to find relative velocities is restricted to motion along one dimension for AP Physics 1.
rationales.C: This skill is covered by the CED (Topic 1.4); it is restricted in scope to one dimension, not excluded entirely.
rationales.D: This specific relative-velocity skill uses algebraic (component or graphical) vector methods in AP Physics 1, not calculus-based vector methods.

stem: A ball moves along the inside of a vertical circular track. At the instant the ball is at the top of the loop, what is the direction of the normal force exerted by the track on the ball? Assume the ball's speed is greater than the minimum speed required to maintain contact with the track (so the normal force is nonzero).

choices.label: A
choices.text: Upward, away from the center of the loop.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Downward, toward the center of the loop.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Horizontal, tangent to the loop at that point.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Zero, regardless of the ball's speed at the top.

rationales.A: This is a documented, common error (only about half of students correctly identify the direction in this exact scenario per the 2024 Chief Reader Report) that comes from over-generalizing the flat-surface habit of "normal force points up" to a curved track, where it does not apply.
rationales.B: At the top of the loop, the center of the circular path is below the ball, and the inside surface of the track can only push the ball away from the track surface — that is, downward, toward the center.
rationales.C: A normal force is, by definition, perpendicular to the surface of contact, not tangent to it.
rationales.D: The normal force is only exactly zero at the minimum speed required to maintain contact; at any higher speed, the normal force is nonzero.

stem: A 10 kg crate rests on a horizontal floor. The coefficient of static friction between the crate and the floor is 0.5, and the coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.3. A horizontal force of 25 N is applied to the crate, and the crate remains at rest. Use g = 10 m/s^2. What is the magnitude of the static friction force acting on the crate?

rationales.A: This is the maximum possible static friction force (mu_s * N = (0.5)(100) = 50 N), but static friction is an inequality (F_f,s <= mu_s*N), not always equal to this maximum — a common error that treats static friction as though it always takes on its largest possible value.
rationales.B: Because the crate remains at rest, it is in equilibrium, so static friction must exactly balance the applied force: 25 N. This is below the maximum possible static friction (50 N), consistent with the CED's inequality relation F_f,s <= mu_s*N.
rationales.C: This is the kinetic friction force (mu_k * N = (0.3)(100) = 30 N), which does not apply here since the crate is not moving relative to the floor.
rationales.D: Static friction cannot be zero here; without a friction force, the unbalanced 25 N applied force would cause the crate to accelerate, contradicting the given information that the crate remains at rest.

stem: According to the AP Physics 1 course framework, interactions between objects or systems that are not in contact (action-at-a-distance forces) are restricted, on the AP Physics 1 Exam, to:

rationales.A: The CED states that the interaction between objects or systems at a distance is limited to gravitational forces in AP Physics 1; electric and magnetic forces are considered in AP Physics 2.
rationales.B: Electric forces at a distance are part of AP Physics 2, not AP Physics 1, according to the CED.
rationales.C: Only gravitational action-at-a-distance forces are within scope for AP Physics 1; electric and magnetic forces belong to AP Physics 2.
rationales.D: Electric forces are not the action-at-a-distance force considered in AP Physics 1 — gravitational force is.

stem: A 5 kg box is pulled across a horizontal floor a distance of 3 m by a constant force of 20 N directed at 40 degrees above the horizontal. Use cos(40 deg) = 0.766 and sin(40 deg) = 0.643. What is the work done on the box by this 20 N force?

rationales.A: This is F*d with no angle factor at all (20 N x 3 m), which ignores that only the component of force parallel to the displacement does work.
rationales.B: W = F*d*cos(theta) = (20 N)(3 m)(0.766) = 45.96 J, which rounds to approximately 46 J. Only the horizontal (parallel-to-displacement) component of the force does work.
rationales.C: This uses sin(40 deg) instead of cos(40 deg): (20)(3)(0.643) = 38.6 J. The parallel component of a force at an angle theta above the displacement direction uses cosine, not sine.
rationales.D: This is incorrect; the force has a nonzero component parallel to the displacement (since 40 degrees is not 90 degrees), so nonzero work is done.

stem: An object moves between two fixed points on a rough horizontal surface. Which of the following statements correctly describes the work done on the object by friction, according to the AP Physics 1 course framework?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is path-independent, like the work done by gravity between the same two points.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It depends on the specific path taken between the two points.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is always zero if the object returns to its exact starting point.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It can be associated with a potential energy function, the same way gravity is associated with gravitational potential energy.

rationales.A: Friction is explicitly named in the CED as a nonconservative force, and nonconservative-force work is path-dependent — unlike gravity, which is conservative and path-independent.
rationales.B: The CED states that the work done by a nonconservative force is path-dependent, and explicitly names friction and air resistance as examples of nonconservative forces.
rationales.C: This zero-net-work-on-a-closed-loop property applies only to conservative forces. Friction is nonconservative, so returning to the starting point does not guarantee zero net work by friction -- the work done depends on the specific path traveled.
rationales.D: The CED states that potential energies are associated only with conservative forces; since friction is nonconservative, no potential energy function can be defined for it.

stem: A 2 kg object's speed increases from 3 m/s to 5 m/s. What is the change in the object's kinetic energy?

rationales.A: This results from incorrectly computing (1/2)m(delta v)^2 = (1/2)(2)(5-3)^2 = 4 J — a documented error pattern that squares the change in speed instead of correctly finding the difference of the squared speeds.
rationales.C: This is only the final kinetic energy, (1/2)(2)(5)^2 = 25 J; it omits subtracting the initial kinetic energy to find the change.
rationales.D: This is only the initial kinetic energy, (1/2)(2)(3)^2 = 9 J, not the change in kinetic energy.

stem: A cyclist exerts a constant force of 40 N parallel to the direction of motion while traveling at an instantaneous speed of 6 m/s along a flat, straight road. What is the instantaneous power output at that moment? (This net force acts on the cyclist-bicycle system.)

rationales.A: For a constant force parallel to velocity, instantaneous power is P = F*v = (40 N)(6 m/s) = 240 W.
rationales.B: This results from dividing force by speed (40/6) instead of multiplying, which does not correspond to the power formula P=Fv.
rationales.C: This is double the correct value, as if the formula included an extra factor of 2 (2Fv) that does not appear in P=Fv.
rationales.D: This results from subtracting speed from force (40-6), which is dimensionally meaningless and does not correspond to the power formula.

stem:
A 1200 kg truck traveling east at 20 m/s collides head-on with a 600 kg car traveling west at 10 m/s. Which of the following correctly compares the magnitude of the truck's change in momentum during the collision to the magnitude of the car's change in momentum during the collision?

A. The truck's change in momentum is twice the car's, because the truck's mass is twice the car's.
B. The truck's change in momentum is half the car's, because the car undergoes the larger acceleration.
C. The magnitudes are equal, and the changes are in opposite directions.
D. The truck's change in momentum is four times the car's, because the truck has four times the initial momentum.

choices.label: A
choices.text: The truck's change in momentum is twice the car's, because the truck's mass is twice the car's.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The truck's change in momentum is half the car's, because the car undergoes the larger acceleration.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The magnitudes are equal, and the changes are in opposite directions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The truck's change in momentum is four times the car's, because the truck has four times the initial momentum.

rationales.A: The mass ratio governs the ratio of the accelerations the two vehicles experience, not the ratio of their momentum changes. Delta-p = F*Delta-t, and both vehicles experience the same force magnitude for the same duration.
rationales.B: The car does undergo the larger acceleration (same force, smaller mass), but acceleration is not momentum change. Multiplying the larger acceleration by the smaller mass returns exactly the same force, and hence exactly the same Delta-p magnitude.
rationales.C: By Newton's third law the two vehicles exert equal-magnitude, opposite forces on each other for the same contact time, so the impulses are equal and opposite. Since impulse equals the change in momentum, the momentum changes are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction -- independent of the masses and speeds.
rationales.D: The initial momenta are indeed 24,000 and 6,000 kg*m/s, a 4:1 ratio, but a momentum change is set by the impulse delivered during the interaction, not by how much momentum an object had beforehand.
